raw_case_text:
A 76-year-old man with a history of peripheral T-cell lymphoma treated with six cycles of cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (CHOP) was referred for abnormal imaging. Initial imaging showed enlarged mediastinal lymphadenopathy, particularly within the right paratracheal and subcarinal regions, as well as prominent mesenteric, retroperitoneal, and pelvic lymphadenopathy. A surveillance computed tomography (CT) of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis performed two months after therapy showed dramatic improvement. However, a new 1.2 cm pulmonary nodule was seen in the superior-medial aspect of the right lower lobe just lateral to the distal bronchus intermedius (Figure 1). A subsequent positron emission tomography-CT (PET-CT) scan revealed this nodule to be hypermetabolic with a standardized uptake value (SUV) of 5.7, raising the suspicion for a possible primary pulmonary malignancy (Figure 2).
The patient underwent bronchoscopy with linear endobronchial ultrasound (EBUS). After passing the scope into the distal bronchus intermedius and rotating the probe to face the posterior wall, the pulmonary nodule was identified on ultrasound. A 22-guage needle was used to obtain tissue. Cytology showed no evidence of malignant cells, and flow cytometry showed no discrete clonal B-cell or atypical T-cell population. No tissue was sent for culture. The patient underwent follow-up CT imaging two months later, which showed an enlargement of the nodule to 1.8 cm and two new 1 cm nodules in the peripheral basal right lower lobe. A repeat EBUS was performed, and the area of interest was identified (Figure 3). A 22-guage needle was used to obtain tissue from the same site; this time, suction was used, and up to fifteen passes with the needle were taken with each aspiration. Rapid on-site evaluation (ROSE) did not confirm the presence of lymphocytes. Cytology was again nondiagnostic. No tissue was sent for culture.
The patient was referred to thoracic surgery. He underwent a right video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) with successful resection of the dominant right hilar nodule and two smaller basilar nodules. Pathology from the dominant nodule revealed multiple necrotizing granulomas, some of which were surrounded by organizing pneumonia (Figure 4). Acid-fast bacilli stain was negative. Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain demonstrated clusters of organisms compatible with Pneumocystis in the center of these granulomas (Figure 5). On follow-up, the patient remained asymptomatic. He declined treatment with trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX) and elected to pursue serial CT scans to monitor for recurrence. A repeat CT chest 6 months later showed no evidence of recurrence.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 76-year-old asymptomatic man in remission 2 months after completing six cycles of CHOP chemotherapy for peripheral T-cell lymphoma was referred for a new 1.2 cm hypermetabolic right lower lobe pulmonary nodule.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had completed six cycles of CHOP chemotherapy (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone) 2 months earlier for peripheral T-cell lymphoma (which had initially presented with extensive right paratracheal, subcarinal, mesenteric, retroperitoneal, and pelvic lymphadenopathy). While restaging thoracoabdominopelvic CT showed dramatic nodal regression, a new 1.2 cm right lower lobe nodule was discovered that demonstrated hypermetabolism (SUV 5.7) on PET-CT, and enlarged to 1.8 cm alongside two new 1.0 cm basilar nodules on 2-month follow-up CT.
subjective.past_medical_history: Peripheral T-cell lymphoma treated with 6 cycles of CHOP chemotherapy completed 2 months prior to referral.
subjective.review_of_systems: Completely asymptomatic from a respiratory and constitutional standpoint.

objective.advanced_workup: Surveillance CT and 18F-FDG PET-CT (2 months post-CHOP): Dramatic resolution of lymphoma-related mediastinal and abdominal lymphadenopathy, but appearance of a new 1.2 cm nodule in the superior-medial right lower lobe lateral to the distal bronchus intermedius with FDG SUVmax of 5.7; repeat CT 2 months later showed growth of the dominant nodule to 1.8 cm plus two new 1.0 cm peripheral right lower lobe basilar nodules. Two sequential linear endobronchial ultrasound-guided transbronchial needle aspirations (EBUS-TBNA, 22G needle): Both procedures yielded nondiagnostic cytology without malignant cells or clonal B/T-cell populations on flow cytometry (tissue was not sent for microbiological culture). Right video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) wedge resection of the dominant right hilar nodule and two smaller basilar nodules: Histopathology demonstrated multiple necrotizing granulomas surrounded by organizing pneumonia, negative acid-fast bacilli (AFB) stain, and clusters of Pneumocystis organisms within the necrotic granuloma centers on Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) stain.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Asymptomatic FDG-avid necrotizing granulomatous Pneumocystis jirovecii pulmonary nodules (1.8 cm dominant right lower lobe nodule and two 1.0 cm basilar nodules; SUVmax 5.7) mimicking primary lung malignancy or lymphoma relapse after six cycles of CHOP chemotherapy for peripheral T-cell lymphoma, definitively diagnosed by VATS wedge resection and Grocott methenamine silver (GMS) staining after two nondiagnostic EBUS-TBNA procedures. Plan and clinical course: Following complete VATS surgical resection of the nodules, the asymptomatic patient declined oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole therapy in favor of active radiographic surveillance, and 6-month follow-up chest CT confirmed no recurrence.
